trainingMethods.overview: For Alzheimer's disease (AD), training methods are primarily used to delay cognitive decline, maintain the ability to perform activities of daily living (ADLs), and improve emotional well-being. Non-pharmacological interventions often yield the best results when combined across multiple dimensions.

methods.name: Reality Orientation Therapy (ROT)
methods.description: Repeatedly guide patients daily to confirm time, location, and person identities using calendars, clocks, weather reports, or family photos to reduce spatio-temporal confusion.

methods.name: Reminiscence Therapy
methods.description: Use old photos, classic songs, or nostalgic items to trigger long-term memory and encourage patients to share stories from their past, which significantly boosts their mood and social engagement.

methods.name: Targeted Memory & Calculation Exercises
methods.description: Engage in simple arithmetic (e.g., addition and subtraction within 100), word associations, picture recognition, playing mahjong, or solving puzzles to stimulate hippocampus and frontal lobe functions.

methods.name: Aerobic Exercise
methods.description: 30 minutes of low-to-moderate intensity daily exercise (such as brisk walking, Tai Chi, Baduanjin, or square dancing) increases cerebral blood flow and oxygen supply while promoting the release of neurotrophic factors.

methods.name: Dual-Task Training
methods.description: Combining physical and cognitive tasks—such as counting while walking or answering simple questions while bouncing a ball—effectively trains the brain's attentional allocation and coordination control.

methods.name: Functional Life Reshaping
methods.description: Breaking down daily activities (such as dressing, brushing teeth, or tidying a desk) into "prompt-demonstrate-assist" steps encourages patients to perform tasks independently and prevents rapid functional decline.

methods.name: Environmental Cue Support
methods.description: Placing prominent text or icon labels on doors (e.g., "Bathroom" or "Bedroom") reduces anxiety caused by spatial disorientation.

methods.name: Music Therapy
methods.description: Playing familiar songs from the patient's youth to guide rhythmic clapping or singing along significantly improves mood swings and mitigates Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia (BPSD).

methods.name: Crafts & Horticulture
methods.description: Fine motor activities like stringing beads, origami, or watering plants maintain hand dexterity while instilling a sense of accomplishment.

principles: The core focus is on maximizing encouragement and minimizing corrections.
Training intensity should dynamically adapt to the patient's disease stage (mild, moderate, or severe) to avoid feelings of frustration and resistance.

executionGuidelines.name: Flexible Adjustments
executionGuidelines.description: If the patient shows signs of fatigue, resistance, or loss of focus, pause the activity immediately—never force engagement.

executionGuidelines.name: Break Down Instructions
executionGuidelines.description: Deliver one simple, concise command at a time (e.g., "Please pick up this brush" rather than multi-step requests).

executionGuidelines.name: Encourage Over Correcting
executionGuidelines.description: Prioritize the pleasure and sense of security derived from participation; refrain from harsh corrections even when mistakes occur.

dailySchedule.overview: For individuals with mild Alzheimer's disease (AD), the daily routine should be structured, balanced between activity and rest, and tailored to a moderate difficulty level. Maintaining a consistent daily rhythm helps minimize anxiety and cognitive confusion.

blocks.goals: Reality Orientation: Guide the patient to check the calendar for the date and weather; encourage independent grooming and dressing.
Coordination & Oxygenation: 30–45 minutes of walking, Tai Chi, or Baduanjin; get sunlight exposure to regulate the circadian rhythm.
Brain Stimulation: Engage in puzzles, simple Sudoku, mahjong, picture recognition, or simple arithmetic (addition/subtraction within 100).
ADL Maintenance: Assign light tasks within their capability, such as sorting vegetables, wiping tables, or folding clothes.
Serve a balanced diet (referencing Mediterranean/MIND diets); allow a 30–45 minute afternoon nap after eating.
Remote Memory & Emotional Support: Look through old photo albums, listen to classic songs, share past stories, or chat with neighbors.
Hand-Brain Coordination & Accomplishment: Water plants, do crafts (origami/beading), draw, or clap along to music.
Dual-Task Training: Practice mental arithmetic while walking slowly, or name fruits while bouncing a ball.
Listen to soothing music, prepare and eat dinner, and keep the environment bright.
Watch light documentaries or news; avoid intense, distressing, or overstimulating media content.
Foot soak, listen to soft music, dim room lights, and encourage falling asleep before 21:30.
